title: How a Request Travels
subtitle: Follow one page load from the Enter key to the last byte, and see which hops eat the time.
learn: What a DNS lookup does and when it is skipped
Why TCP and TLS setup cost round trips before any data moves
The path browser → load balancer → app server → database and back
Why distance and slow queries dominate page load time

steps.title: You press Enter
steps.body: You type shop.example and press Enter. Roughly half a second later a page appears. That half second is not one thing: it is a chain of separate conversations between machines, and each one has to finish before the next can start. This lesson walks the chain in order and times each link.
steps.idea: A page load is a sequence of dependent waits; the total is their sum.
steps.caption: The browser knows a name, not an address.

steps.title: Find the address
steps.body: Computers route by IP address, so the browser first asks a DNS resolver which address belongs to shop.example. If the answer is already cached in the browser, the OS, or the resolver, this costs almost nothing. A cold lookup can walk root, TLD, and authoritative servers and take tens of milliseconds.
steps.idea: DNS answers are cached according to their TTL; a warm cache makes this step nearly free.
steps.caption: Resolver returns an IP address.

steps.title: Open a secure connection
steps.body: Before sending the request the browser opens a TCP connection (one round trip) and negotiates TLS encryption (one more round trip with TLS 1.3). No page data moves yet. If the server is 50 ms away, that is already about 100 ms spent just agreeing to talk.
steps.idea: Handshakes cost round trips, so physical distance multiplies directly into latency.
steps.caption: TCP + TLS handshakes complete.

steps.title: Send the request
steps.body: The browser sends GET / with headers and cookies. A load balancer receives it and forwards it to one healthy app server. The load balancer exists so any single server can fail or be replaced without the user noticing.
steps.idea: The load balancer hides how many servers exist and which one answers.
steps.caption: Request forwarded to an app server.

steps.title: Fetch the data
steps.body: The app server runs the handler, which usually needs data: the product list, the user's cart, prices. It queries the database. A well-indexed query returns in a few milliseconds; the handler then renders HTML or JSON from the rows.
steps.idea: Server time is application logic plus every dependency it waits on.
steps.caption: App queries the database.

steps.title: Bytes come back
steps.body: The HTML travels back through the load balancer to the browser. The first byte arriving (time to first byte, TTFB) is a common health metric. The browser starts parsing immediately, before the whole response has downloaded.
steps.idea: TTFB captures everything up to here: DNS, connect, and server time.
steps.caption: HTML streams back to the browser.

steps.title: More files
steps.body: The HTML references CSS, JavaScript, fonts, and images. The browser fetches these too, usually from a CDN edge server close to the user, reusing connections and downloading several in parallel. Static files are cached aggressively so repeat visits skip most of this.
steps.idea: Serving static assets from the edge removes distance from most of the bytes.
steps.caption: Static assets arrive from a nearby edge.

steps.title: A slow query
steps.body: Suppose the product query scans the whole table instead of using an index and takes 900 ms. Every other step is unchanged, yet the page now takes over a second. One slow dependency on the critical path dominates the whole request, which is why you measure each hop instead of guessing.
steps.idea: The slowest hop on the critical path sets the user's experience.
steps.caption: The database is now the bottleneck.

steps.title: A faraway user
steps.body: Now put the user on another continent, 150 ms away. Each round trip costs 150 ms, so the handshakes alone cost about 300 ms and the request another 150 ms. Code cannot fix the speed of light; moving servers or caches closer to users can.
steps.idea: Latency from distance is paid per round trip, so fewer round trips and closer servers both help.
steps.caption: Each round trip now costs 150 ms.

steps.title: Where the time went
steps.body: A request is DNS, connect, request, server work, response, and assets, in that order. Caching cuts DNS and asset time, connection reuse cuts handshakes, indexes cut server time, and CDNs or regional servers cut distance. To make a page faster, first find which hop is slow.
steps.idea: Measure each hop, then fix the biggest one.
steps.caption: Every hop added to the total.

quiz.q: A page's DNS lookup takes 0 ms on a repeat visit. What is the most likely reason?
options: DNS is skipped for HTTPS sites
The answer was cached and its TTL had not expired
The load balancer stores IP addresses
quiz.why: Resolvers, the OS, and browsers cache DNS answers until their TTL expires, so repeat lookups are near-instant.

quiz.q: The server is 80 ms away (round trip). Roughly how long do a fresh TCP + TLS 1.3 handshake take before the request can be sent?
quiz.why: TCP needs one round trip and TLS 1.3 needs one more, so about two round trips: 2 × 80 ms.

quiz.q: TTFB jumps from 200 ms to 1.2 s after a deploy, but DNS and connect times are unchanged. Where should you look first?
options: Server-side work such as a slow database query
quiz.why: If DNS and connection setup are unchanged, the added time is inside the server's handling, typically a slow dependency like a query.

cheatsheet.def: Round-trip time: how long a message takes to reach a server and come back. Handshakes cost whole RTTs.
Time to first byte: from sending the request until the first response byte arrives. Includes DNS, connect, and server time.
One round trip to agree on keys (zero with session resumption) before encrypted data can flow.
The chain of steps that must finish in order; its slowest step bounds total latency.
